newsitem.title: USA: U.S. retailers rail against Canadian lumber quotas.
newsitem.headline: U.S. retailers rail against Canadian lumber quotas.

text.p: U.S. lumber retailers, feeling rebuffed by the Federal Trade Commission, said Thursday they were writing their congressmen to have an agreement setting quotas on Canadian lumber exports changed.

"We're having our members send letters writing their congressmen and senators asking for public hearings to be held before the Ways and Means committee. We would at least like it to be tweaked a little bit to have more flexibility," said Rita Ferris, director of legislative and regulatory affairs at the Northeastern Retail Lumber Association (NRLA).

A Dec 3 meeting with the trade commission and Canadian embassy officials in Washington proved unsatisfactory, Ferris said, explaining the officials blamed any problems on "this just being the agreement's first year."
She said, "They expect price stability to return this year, but our members aren't so sure."
Some 8,000 participants are expected at the three-day NRLA conference in Boston that began Thursday.
"The quotas have established a great deal of uncertainty," NRLA chairman Michael Fritz said. "The problem isn't the price - though we would like to see it lowered - price stability is the problem."
He estimated the spike in lumber prices between Oct 30 and Nov 25 cut the profits of his family-owned Rugg Lumber Co in Greenfield, Massachusetts by 20 percent for 1996.
Fritz expected price volatility to continue as long as the quotas remain unchanged.
"There is a lack of understanding, especially by the people on this side of the border, about these quotas," Fritz said.

From April 1, Canadian lumber exports that exceed quarterly or annual quotas are subject to export fees. Exports above 14.7 billion board feet annually or 4.226 billion board feet quarterly are subject to US$50 fee for every 1,000 board feet. If such excess exports exceed 650 million board feet, they are subject to a US$100 fee for every 1,000 board feet.
Export quotas are allocated for each province on a company-by-company basis. Shippers who have not been given an allocation are subject to the US$100 fee for any lumber they export.

Fritz said he expected home sales to remain flat in the northeast with a possible decline in lower price starts in part because some Canadian mills, nearing their quotas have in some cases stopped shipping lower priced products. He said he delivered several frames for houses Monday and Tuesday during what has been a relatively mild winter with little snow on the ground in New England.
